title.en: The game that night always wins

text.en: Every evening, children run around a field until it gets too dark to see. In this tiny poem by Georgia Heard, who wins the game? It is not any child. Let us read between the lines.

Think about when you go to play after school, who you play with, where, and when you come back home. The poem is about an evening game of ball played by children, so it is about playing, running and the end of the day.
The speaker and friends play ball in the evenings next to a creek, in the neighbour's field. A creek is a small body of water. They run so fast that the speaker cannot catch her breath, which shows that they are tired from running, and that the speaker is not alone because the poem says we. As the sky turns from blue to black the children feel the cold grass making their feet ache. The trees seem to creep close in the dark. At last the game is over, because it is dark, and the poet announces that night is the winner.
The sky changing from blue to black tells us that the colour of the sky changes as evening becomes night. Trees seem to creep close because in the dark they look larger and nearer, and it is hard to see far. The grass is cold because the evening is cold and the dew has fallen, so the children's feet ache. The night wins because the time for play has ended and it is time to go home.
Repetition, as in a pattern repeating a word, can highlight a feeling. Example: the leaves are falling, falling, falling. Personification gives human qualities to things that are not alive. The night is shown as a winner of a game, even though night cannot win. Another example: the sun played hide-and-seek with the clouds. Try writing your own example of each device.
A creek is one water body. Others are a pond, lake, river, stream, sea, ocean, canal and well. Think about which ones you can find near your home. Creating a word web of water bodies is a good way to remember them.
Run and pass, kick a black and white ball into the goal and watch out for mud: this is football. Hold your breath and say hu-tu-tu while touching players and running back to your side: this is kabaddi. Arms turn, legs kick in a cool blue pool: this is swimming. Breathe in, breathe out, practise daily to be healthy, fit and full of energy: this is yoga. You can create a riddle about your favourite game too.
In pairs, act a parent and child: coming home late from play, sharing the games you played, and bringing a new friend home. Write a paragraph on your playtime: when you go out, who you play with, what games, your favourite game, what you gain and when you go home. Give it a title. Indigenous games are native to a region. Kho-kho is an example. Find out games from your state, learn the rules and play one with your teacher's supervision.

problem.en: Explain the meaning of the line about trees creeping close.

text.en: Think about the time of day in the poem.

why.en: It is evening, turning to night.

text.en: In the dark the trees look nearer and bigger, so they seem to creep closer.

why.en: That is a picture of the darkness arriving.

problem.en: Find the personification in the poem.

text.en: Look for something not alive acting like a person.

why.en: Personification gives human qualities to non-living things.

text.en: Night is described as winning a game, which only people can do.

prompt.en: Explain why night is called the winner in the poem and what the poem tells about the children.

requiredIdeas.en: The children were playing happily in the evening.
They were out of breath from running.
Darkness and cold ended the game.
Night wins because it is time to go home.

commonMisconceptions.en: The child who ran fastest won.
The game ended because it rained.

points.en: The Winner is a short poem by Georgia Heard about an evening game.
The children play ball by a creek until dark.
The night wins as it brings the game to an end.
The poem uses repetition and personification.
A creek is a small body of water.
